I keep a small, battered notebook on my desk that I call the Book of Unfinished Things.

It's not a journal, not really. It doesn't have dates on the pages, or neat entries. It's a catchment for half-thoughts. Sentences that wandered in at 2 a.m. and left before I could offer them a chair. Sketches of inventions that will never exist. The first line of a story I know I'll never finish: "When Mara finally taught her house to breathe, it exhaled all the guests."

I bought it for $4 at a drugstore. The cover is a faded teal color that has been bleached by the sun on one side because I left it on my windowsill for a summer. Most of the pages are still empty. That, I think, is the point.

We live in a world that is obsessed with finishing. With closure. With productivity systems and life hacks and ten-step plans to complete your novel in thirty days. Everything needs to be wrapped up, monetized, shipped, posted, and archived. The unfinished thing feels like a failure, a debt, a moral lapse.

But I have come to believe that the unfinished is where most of life actually happens.

Think about it. The conversations you remember aren't the ones that ended neatly with everyone agreeing. They are the ones that trailed off because someone laughed too hard, or the waiter interrupted, or the bus arrived. The songs you love aren't loved because they are technically complete; they are loved because of that one unresolved chord that makes your chest ache a little. Even the universe itself is, as far as we can tell, unfinished. It is still expanding. It is still cooling. It hasn't decided what it wants to be when it grows up.

I want to write freely today about that feeling — the feeling of living in the middle.

---

We are taught to think of time as an arrow. It flies in one direction, from past to future, and we are somewhere along its shaft, hurtling forward. But lived time doesn't feel like an arrow at all. It feels more like a tide pool.

When you were a kid, did you ever crouch over a tide pool and watch it? At first it looks like a separate little world, self-contained, still. But if you sit long enough you see it is anything but still. A hermit crab drags a shell an inch to the left. Algae shivers. A tiny fish darts and then freezes, pretending it is a rock. Water from the larger ocean sighs in over the edge every few minutes, refreshes everything, and then retreats. The tide pool is both separate from the ocean and completely at its mercy. It is both waiting and happening.

That is how a human day feels to me now. We have our little self-contained pools — our apartments, our commutes, our routines, our carefully curated playlists — but the ocean is always sighing over the edge. A news headline. A sudden memory of someone who died ten years ago triggered by the smell of rain on hot pavement. A phone call that changes everything.

We pretend we are in control of the pool. We buy pool cleaners and test the pH and arrange the little decorative rocks. But the ocean does what it wants.

I used to fight that. I used to make five-year plans. In college I had a color-coded spreadsheet of my entire life until age 40. It included things like "learn conversational Japanese" and "run a marathon" and "get promoted" in neat quarterly blocks. I look at it now and laugh, not unkindly. Past-me was so earnest. Past-me really thought you could spreadsheet the tide.

What I didn't understand then is that the most interesting hermit crabs arrive precisely when you aren't looking. The best conversations happen when you miss your train. The person you end up loving is rarely the person who matched all the criteria on your spreadsheet.

So now, instead of a five-year plan, I have a practice. Every morning I sit for ten minutes and do nothing. Not meditate, exactly. Not in the incense-and-chanting way. I just sit. I let the pool settle. I watch the light move across the wall. I notice the way my mind tries to immediately start planning, worrying, listing. I don't stop it. I just watch it, the way you would watch that hermit crab. "Ah, there goes the worry about the email I haven't answered. There goes the fantasy about moving to a cabin in Norway."

It sounds small, even pointless. But it has changed everything. Because for ten minutes a day, I am not trying to finish anything.

---

There's a word I love that I learned a few years ago: "Sonder." It's a neologism, coined not by ancient Greeks but by a modern writer, John Koenig, in his Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows. Sonder is the realization that each random passerby is living a life as vivid and complex as your own — populated with their own ambitions, friends, routines, worries, and inherited craziness.

You are the main character of your own story, absolutely. But so is the woman bagging your groceries. So is the teenage boy on the skateboard who almost knocks you over. So is the man on the bus who is crying quietly while looking out the window.

If you really let sonder hit you, it is vertiginous. Standing on a busy street corner in any city and letting it in properly feels like leaning over a great height. All those worlds, layered on top of each other, invisible but entirely real.

I try to practice sonder deliberately. Sometimes when I'm on the subway I will pick one person — not to stare, but to imagine, gently, respectfully. That older man with the careful, trimmed beard and the plastic bag full of what looks like oranges. Where is he going? Maybe he's bringing them to his grandchildren. Maybe he always brings oranges on Thursdays. Maybe his wife used to tell him he bought the wrong kind of oranges and now he stands in the produce aisle for a long time, trying to remember which ones she liked, and the oranges are a kind of apology.

I will never know. I don't need to know. The point isn't to be right. The point is to remember that the world is not a backdrop for my life. I am a background extra in thousands of other films.

This practice has made me kinder, I think. Or at least less annoyed. It's hard to be furious at someone for walking slowly when you remember they are carrying an entire universe in their head. It's hard to dehumanize anyone when you remember that they, too, have a Book of Unfinished Things somewhere.

And it has made me less lonely. Because loneliness, I think, comes not from being alone, but from the illusion that you are alone in your aloneness. Sonder reminds you that everyone is alone together, in separate tide pools connected by the same ocean.

---

A few months ago I was walking in the woods behind my house. It had rained the night before, hard. The trail was muddy and the air smelled like wet bark and turned earth, that rich, fungal, alive smell. I wasn't listening to anything. No podcast, no music. Just walking.

And I noticed something I had never noticed before, even though I've walked that trail hundreds of times: the sound of water, everywhere, but not from a stream. The forest was dripping. Every leaf, every branch, was holding a little of last night's rain and then, according to its own private rhythm, letting it fall. Plip. Plip-plip. Plip. Thousands of tiny, asynchronous drips.

I stopped and just stood there for maybe five minutes. It was a percussion ensemble with no conductor. No pattern that I could discern, but not random either. Each drip was the result of a precise sequence: how the leaf was curved, how much water it had collected, how the wind brushed it.

I felt, in that moment, a kind of click in my understanding. I have spent so much of my life looking for the melody — the big, grand narrative, the arc, the meaning of it all — that I had missed the percussion. The texture. The drips.

We are drip creatures. Our lives are not symphonies, most days. They are drips. Making coffee. Answering an email. Holding the door. Texting a friend a meme. Small, unremarkable actions that, in aggregate, make a sound, make a world.

There is a Japanese concept called "wabi-sabi" that has no perfect English translation, but roughly means finding beauty in imperfection, impermanence, and incompleteness. A cracked bowl mended with gold. Moss growing on stone. The asymmetry of a handmade cup.

The dripping forest was wabi-sabi. The Book of Unfinished Things is wabi-sabi. A life that is not optimized or complete but noticed — that is wabi-sabi.

I wonder what would happen if we taught wabi-sabi in schools. Alongside math and history, a class where you just learn to notice. To mend a broken thing with gold. To sit with something that isn't finished and not rush to fix it.

---

Let me tell you a story I haven't finished.

There is a lighthouse keeper — let's call her Elara — who tends a lighthouse that no longer guides any ships. The coast has shifted over a hundred years, the shipping lanes have moved, and now the light sweeps uselessly over a field of dry grass and a single, lonely highway. But Elara stays anyway, because her father kept it before her, and his mother before him. She polishes the brass. She winds the mechanism. Every night at dusk, she climbs the 97 iron steps and turns the light on, and it goes around and around, illuminating the grasshoppers and the billboards and the occasional truck.

People in town think she's eccentric, or sad. They say, "Elara, why don't you come down? No one needs it."

One night, a storm knocks out the power for miles. The highway is dark. The town is dark. The drivers on the highway can't see the curve where the road bends sharply around the old cliff. And Elara's light — which is on its own old generator — is the only light for miles. It sweeps, and sweeps, and a truck driver sees it just in time and turns. He doesn't know what it was. He thinks it was a strange, low star.

Elara never knows she saved anyone. The next morning the power comes back on and the town goes back to thinking she's eccentric. She polishes the brass.

I don't know how that story ends. Maybe it doesn't end. Maybe that's the point. Maybe Elara's job isn't about being needed. Maybe it's about tending.

I think about her a lot when I'm doing the small, unthanked things. Doing the dishes when no one will see. Writing a note I'll never send. Being kind to someone who will never remember my name.

Tending is not impressive. It rarely gets applause. But it is, I think, the most human thing we do. We tend. We keep the light on even when no ships are coming, because keeping the light on is itself a kind of prayer. It says: I was here. I cared for this thing. I kept it ready.

---

If you have read this far, thank you. We have spent a little while together in this tide pool. I don't know who you are, or what time it is where you are, or what is unfinished in your life that is weighing on you.

Perhaps it is a relationship. Perhaps it is a work project. Perhaps it is grief. Perhaps it is just laundry.

Whatever it is, I want to offer you a small permission slip, from one keeper of unfinished things to another:

You do not have to finish it today.

You are allowed to be in the middle. The middle is not a failure. The middle is where the drips are. The middle is where the hermit crab is dragging its borrowed house across the sand, slowly, with great effort, for no reason that will ever make the news.

You are allowed to tend to your light even if no one sees it.

If you like, close your eyes for a minute after you finish reading this. Listen to the drips in your own forest. The heater humming. The distant traffic. Your own breath. The unfinished sentence in your own notebook.

Let it be unfinished for a little longer.

It will keep.

---

A final thought, because I promised myself I would write freely and this is where my mind is going, unedited: I think the reason we fear unfinished things is that they remind us of mortality. A finished book can be shelved. A finished life can be eulogized. But an unfinished thing is vulnerable. It is still open to wind and rain and change. It says, "I have not yet become."

And that is terrifying, because it means we have not yet become, either. We are all drafts. We are all revisions in progress. There is no final, perfect, polished version of us that will one day be unveiled to applause. There is just this version, today, dripping a little, polishing the brass, remembering to bring oranges.

And that, strangely, is not sad at all. It is hopeful. It means there is still time to add a line to the notebook. To take another walk. To let the ocean sigh over the edge of our little pool and bring something unexpected.

So here is my wish for you, whoever you are, on whatever Thursday this finds you: May you have something unfinished that you love enough to tend. May you notice one small, beautiful drip today that you would have otherwise missed. And may you be gentle with your own becoming.

Turn the light on tonight, even if no one is watching.

It matters.
